title: Four Ministers Pledge a Coordination Center in the Philippines. One by That Name Already Exists
dek: The Oct. 28 pledge follows two years in which the United States and the Philippines built and exercised a center under that name. The public record points to a change in who takes part and what they can see, not in who commands, with the rules for sharing classified information setting the limit.

body_paragraphs.text: The defense ministers of Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States have committed to “establishing a Combined Coordination Center (CCC) in the Philippines.” The pledge appears in a
joint statement
on their Oct. 28 meeting in Cebu, on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus. Australia’s defence ministers posted it on Nov. 10, and Japan’s Ministry of Defense published the
Japanese text

the same day. Neither version says where the center will be, how it will be organized or when it will open. A center by that name already exists at Camp Aguinaldo, the headquarters of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) in Quezon City. It was built with the United States and used by the multinational force in this year’s Balikatan exercise.

The center heads a list of four initiatives, alongside synchronizing defense investments for the Philippines’ archipelagic defense, closer policy consultations and expanded combined exercises. The statement says they build on the recently signed Terms of Reference of the four countries’ Pacific Chiefs of Defense Cooperation Council (DCC) and on exercises such as Balikatan and Keen Sword. The Philippine Department of National Defense (DND) released the statement on Nov. 10 without further detail on the center’s location, structure, timeline or functions,
Manila Bulletin reported
. The idea did not appear in the
joint readout
of the ministers’ previous meeting, in Kuala Lumpur in November 2025, which discussed information sharing, joint training and operational coordination.
Nor did it appear in Japan’s account on the day of the meeting. The Ministry of Defense’s
readout
recorded Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s proposal to strengthen policy consultations. At his
news conference

that night, neither his opening remarks nor the questions that followed mentioned a coordination center. He noted that all three of Japan’s partners in the meeting hold acquisition and cross-servicing agreements (ACSAs) with Japan, and said he and Teodoro would work toward an agreement on protecting classified military information. Thirteen days later the ministry published the statement that lists the center first. Neither document shows what role, if any, the Self-Defense Forces would have in it.
The name predates the pledge. A
U.S. military account of Balikatan 25

described that exercise as building on “the previous iteration’s Combined Coordination Center,” which in 2024 had synchronized separate Philippine and U.S. joint task forces. In November 2024, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III and Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
broke ground
on a new combined coordination center at Camp Aguinaldo during the visit on which the two countries signed a General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA). A Department of Defense
fact sheet
said the center would improve bilateral operational planning and let U.S. and Philippine forces work side by side in response to real-time incidents, “including those in the South China Sea.”
During Balikatan 25, in April 2025, a
U.S. exercise report

described the CCC at Camp Aguinaldo as “a secure, joint operations node” where planners and directors from both countries aligned their activities while each side ran its own joint task force. That was an exercise arrangement, a year before the center was described as new. At the close of Balikatan 2026 on May 8, Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM), said the entire multinational force had “embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center.” His words were reported by the
Indo-Pacific Defense Forum
, a publication INDOPACOM sponsors, whose staff article placed the center at Camp Aguinaldo and described it as a hub between the AFP and INDOPACOM for multinational coordination.
Other accounts point to more than one site and to U.S. money.
USNI News reported

that the exercise network ran from new combined coordination centers throughout the Philippines, funded by the United States through programs including the Pacific Deterrence Initiative and staffed by combined American and Filipino teams. Japan sent about 1,400 troops to its first Balikatan as a participant, and
INDOPACOM listed
Australia among the participating countries.
This week’s accounts differ on whether the four-country center exists. The statement speaks of establishing it, and
Manila Standard

described it on Nov. 12 as still planned. Asked about it on Nov. 11, Teodoro said, “There will be a coordination mechanism. Right now, it is already operating,” adding that locations could be disclosed once the parties agreed,
GMA News reported
. GMA’s summary placed the center in Manila, which his quoted words did not. The
Inquirer
noted that he did not say whether the mechanism was the facility used in Balikatan or a separate arrangement.

Three readings fit the record: the Camp Aguinaldo center placed under a four-party arrangement; a network of sites, consistent with the plural in the U.S. accounts and Teodoro’s reference to locations; or a new body that reuses a familiar name. As of Nov. 13, the statements and remarks reviewed here did not say which. The bilateral center and the four-country pledge are therefore not established to be identical. But the bilateral center is the only working model on the public record, and it indicates what regular Japanese and Australian participation could change.

The first change would be in who is in the room. The center on the record has been bilateral in its staffing: a U.S. deputy director and a Philippine liaison officer in Balikatan 25, combined American and Filipino teams in 2026. None of these sources says whether Japanese or Australian officers were posted to the center itself. Regular participation would replace exercise-period involvement with standing liaison officers from four militaries, each reporting to its own chain of command.

The second is a matter of what would not change. In Balikatan 25 the center kept “both commanders” informed, in the words of its U.S. deputy director, while each country ran its own task force. That is coordination of parallel national forces, not a multinational command, and the ministers’ statement uses no command language. Paparo’s reference to future Balikatan exercises led “through coalition combined command centers” is one U.S. commander’s forward-looking description, not a commitment by the four governments. What each force may do would still be decided nationally, and the legal ground on the record is bilateral: in Kuala Lumpur the four ministers
applauded
the entry into force of the Japan–Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement, and on Oct. 28 Koizumi spoke of
turning that agreement and the ACSAs into concrete unit operations
. Australia’s arrangements with the Philippines are outside the sources reviewed here.

The third and most binding is information. The GSOMIA that the United States and the Philippines signed in 2024 is bilateral; it covers classified military information shared between those two governments. Japan and the Philippines are still working toward an equivalent, Koizumi said on Oct. 28. Balikatan 2026 handled the difference through a U.S. system:
INDOPACOM said

its common operating picture was open to eight nations, with foreign disclosure officers helping tag data so it could cross between networks. In that design, what a Japanese or Australian officer can see on a U.S. network turns on U.S. release decisions. The sources reviewed here document no four-country instrument for classified information. That is a gap in the public record, not a finding that relevant arrangements among the four do not exist.
The fourth is planning, where the larger question lies. The 2024 fact sheet gave the bilateral center a role in real-time incidents, not only exercises.
GMA reported

that Teodoro described interoperability requirements as no longer limited to education and training, and that coordination of military exercises had moved from the AFP Education and Training Command to Strategic Command. In Kuala Lumpur the ministers had
welcomed
plans for Balikatan 2026 with forces from all four countries, and now pledge larger and more frequent combined exercises. The DCC Terms of Reference, which
Manila Bulletin

says include information sharing and interoperability in planning, could frame that work; their text is not among the sources reviewed. The statements reviewed here do not say whether the four-country center inherits the incident role or remains an exercise-planning node.
The fifth is money.
USNI reported

that the United States paid for the centers used in Balikatan 2026, including through the Pacific Deterrence Initiative. The statement’s pledge to synchronize defense investments for the Philippines’ archipelagic defense does not say who would fund a four-country center, and nothing in the record shows Japan or Australia paying for one.

Taken together, the record supports a narrower and more concrete reading than the pledge invites. On the demonstrated model, a four-country CCC would not place four militaries under one command. It would give Japan and Australia a standing place in a coordination structure the United States and the Philippines built, reached largely through U.S. networks and U.S. release decisions. The change that would matter most is functional, not physical: whether a structure designed in 2024 partly for real-time incidents, including in the South China Sea, takes on that role for four countries outside exercises, and whether a Japan–Philippines information agreement lets Japan see enough to take part. The public record shows neither yet.
